acquisition.why: This depends on an existing large audience (1.5M followers) and founder-led content, which Ricardo does not have. Paid Meta ads to a cold audience are legal and agent-manageable, but conversion without a personal brand is weak [E].

onboarding.why: Checkout and course-platform access can run unattended (Kajabi/Teachable/Gumroad).

delivery.why: The live weekly webinar plus contractor-run upsells needs a human presenter. Recorded courses would score higher but convert worse.

support.why: Agents can handle access and refund queries. Course-quality complaints need human review.

scores.R_why: The idea needs an established personal brand and audience plus 2 hrs/week of live webinars. Ricardo has no audience, and £300 buys little Meta ad testing. The £250k/month claim is unverified, from one creator, with currency not stated.
scores.M_why: 'Learn AI video/social' courses are extremely saturated in 2026. Free YouTube content and AI tools themselves substitute for them, and buyers are wary of guru products.
scores.one_line: This is an audience-leveraged guru product. Without a 1.5M following it is a crowded, trust-dependent sell that agents can't bootstrap; poor fit.

acquisition.why: Organic content is inbound and legal, and agents can draft posts and newsletters. But reach depends on the creator's authentic voice, and claimed reach is collapsing (50 vs 3–4k followers per post).

onboarding.why: Newsletter or community signup is self-serve.

delivery.why: The core asset is the operator's personal experience and on-camera presence. Faceless AI content struggles in the business/AI niche [E].

billing.why: Sponsorships need some negotiation. Product and subscription billing is automated.

support.why: Mostly community moderation and email, which agents can partly cover.

scores.R_why: Ricardo is technical and could document AI-agent builds, which is authentic material. But 6–8 h/week is thin for building an audience, the payoff takes 12+ months, and the cited $3–7M results come from established operators.
scores.M_why: The AI-educator creator space is heavily saturated, and platform reach is declining. Monetisation depends on scale he won't reach quickly.
scores.one_line: This is well corroborated across 6 videos, but it is a slow, personality-driven audience play. Its only merit is as a long-term distribution channel layered on another business.

acquisition.why: Campaigns are found on marketplaces (Whop/Content Rewards); no outreach is needed. It is fully platform-dependent.

onboarding.why: You join a campaign self-serve via the platform.

delivery.why: AI clipping tools (Opus/Vugola) plus scheduling can automate most of it. But winning clips need taste, and platforms may ban bot-run accounts.

billing.why: The platform pays per view automatically.

support.why: There is minimal client support; it is platform-mediated.

scores.R_why: There is near-zero cost and it can be tested within £300 and a few hours a week; UK residents can use Whop. But income is unproven (the host gives no figures), and posting needs warmed social accounts.
scores.M_why: Clipping is massively crowded and AI clipping commoditises supply, so CPMs compress. TikTok/IG crack down on automated reposting accounts, and campaign terms can change at will.
scores.one_line: It is cheap and highly automatable, but it's a race-to-the-bottom gig on others' platforms with no evidence of meaningful earnings. It is only worth a tiny agent experiment.

acquisition.why: This needs either your own large audience or partnership deals with big creators. That means human-led B2B pitching (creators often trade as sole traders/individuals, so cold DMs are PECR-risky).

delivery.why: Layout can be AI-generated from video content, and print-on-demand mail partners exist. But it is physical print/post with editorial QA [E].

support.why: Physical delivery issues (lost or damaged issues, address changes) generate tickets, plus creator relationship management.

scores.R_why: The quilting example worked because of an existing 10k+ audience. The platform version needs creator deals, rights agreements and print/fulfilment setup. UK postage raises unit costs well beyond the 80¢ print cost claimed, and £300 won't fund a print run.
scores.M_why: Few players turn creator content into print; it is a nostalgia niche with some differentiation. But demand is narrow and creator-dependent.
scores.one_line: This is an interesting niche with a real first-hand anecdote, but it hinges on landing creator partnerships and physical fulfilment. It is too human- and capital-heavy for an agent-run £300 test.

acquisition.why: Inbound via social platforms. Algorithmic reach for AI-cloned content is unreliable.

onboarding.why: There are no customers to onboard if it is for your own channels.

delivery.why: Trend research, generation and posting are largely automatable with current tools.

billing.why: There is no defined monetisation model. Revenue would come from creator funds, affiliates or ads, each needing setup and thresholds.

scores.R_why: It is technically easy for Ricardo and fits the budget. But it is a tactic rather than a business: no customer, no price. Copying viral formats risks copyright and platform AI-content penalties.
scores.M_why: Every creator now has the same tools. AI-slop saturation and platform demotion of low-originality content are intensifying in 2026.
scores.one_line: This is a production tactic with no revenue model, and the evidence is a tool demo (the '3-minute trend scan'). It is commoditised and not a standalone business.

acquisition.why: Buyers find the clips via marketplace search on Pond5/Adobe Stock; no outreach is needed. It is fully platform-dependent.

delivery.why: Generation, metadata and upload can be agent-run. Some quality review is needed to pass marketplace moderation.

scores.R_why: It fits the budget (a Veo/Kling subscription), the hours and Ricardo's skills, and is UK-accessible. But per-download royalties are tiny [E]. Several marketplaces restrict or label AI content (e.g. Adobe accepts it with labels; others limit it).
scores.M_why: Stock libraries are being flooded with AI clips while buyers increasingly generate their own. This is a classic commoditised, shrinking margin.
scores.one_line: It is almost fully automatable and cheap to test, but zero first-hand evidence plus AI self-substitution by buyers make returns likely negligible.

acquisition.why: Not a business: there are no customers. It is a personal investment thesis.

onboarding.why: Not applicable; there is no customer.

delivery.why: Holding shares is passive, but it is not a service.

billing.why: There is no revenue from customers.

scores.R_why: This is a concentrated speculative stock bet on US franchises. £300 is irrelevant at this scale. Turning it into a business (advice or signals) would trigger FCA regulation.
scores.M_why: It is a public-market thesis already priced by institutions, and the outcome depends on a speculative sale.
scores.one_line: This is an investment opinion, not an agent-runnable business. The claims are second-hand valuation guesses, so it should be excluded.

acquisition.why: It works via YouTube, social content or an existing audience built on credibility as an operator. Paid ads are possible, but the playbook needs proof of real operating experience Ricardo lacks.

onboarding.why: Purchase and course access are self-serve.

delivery.why: Recorded content or a PDF is automated once made. Community/coaching elements need a human.

support.why: Buyers expect operator Q&A, and the community needs human expertise.

scores.R_why: The credibility comes from having run the business (stump grinding, tree service). Ricardo has no such operating track record. AI-written playbooks without experience risk being low quality and drawing CMA/ASA scrutiny over earnings claims.
scores.M_why: There is niche demand for specific UK trade playbooks, and some UK-local gaps exist [E]. But the broader info-product market is crowded and buyers distrust it.
scores.one_line: This is well corroborated (9 videos) as a monetisation layer for experienced operators. It suits Ricardo only after he runs a business worth teaching, possibly an agent-run one.
